subject: 심사전과 낙선전
title: The exhibition of what the jury rejected
content: When an official salon rejected an unusually large number of submissions in 1863, the resulting complaints were loud enough that an emperor ordered the rejected works shown separately. The exhibition that followed became one of the more consequential events in the history of European painting, and it did so partly by accident. The jury system had real power. A body of established painters decided what the public would see, rejection could end a career, and the criteria applied were those the jurors had been trained in decades earlier. Complaints about conservatism were continuous and largely ineffective, since there was no alternative venue of comparable standing. Showing the rejected work changed that. Visitors came in large numbers, partly to mock, and the pictures they mocked included several now regarded as central to the period. The exhibition demonstrated that a jury's verdict was a judgment rather than a fact, and once that had been publicly shown it could not be unshown. Independent exhibitions followed within a decade. Artists organised their own shows, without juries, admitting anybody who paid a fee, and the movements that dominated the following half century emerged from exactly those arrangements. The official body continued and steadily lost authority. What the episode established was a pattern that has repeated since. An institution controlling access accumulates a settled taste, work outside that taste accumulates outside the institution, and eventually a parallel structure forms and the older body finds itself judging a narrower field. The same sequence has occurred in publishing, in music, and in film, usually without an emperor to accelerate it.

subject: 의자 디자인이라는 문제
title: Why a chair is so hard to get right
content: A chair must hold a body of unpredictable size in a posture that stays comfortable for an unknown period, be light enough to move, strong enough not to fail, and cheap enough to buy. Designers describe it as the hardest ordinary object, and the number of attempts in any furniture collection supports them. The body defies a single solution. People differ in height, in the length of their limbs relative to their torso, and in how they prefer to sit, so a chair fitted precisely to average dimensions fits almost nobody well. Adjustability solves this at the cost of complexity and expense, which is why office chairs adjust and dining chairs do not. Duration changes the requirement. A chair that is comfortable for ten minutes may be unbearable after two hours, since the body needs to shift and a shape that supports one posture prevents others. Designers of seating for long use therefore aim to permit movement rather than to hold a position, which is the opposite of what looks supportive. Structure fights lightness. The load passes through the joints where the legs meet the seat, and that junction is where chairs fail, so every gain in lightness must be paid for in the joint. The famous designs of the past century are largely solutions to this problem — bent wood, tubular steel, moulded shells — and each new material produced a new family of forms. Cultural expectation completes the difficulty. A chair carries meaning about formality, status, and occasion, and a design that solves every physical problem while looking wrong for its setting will not be bought, which designers describe as the constraint they can least argue with.

subject: 자동 인형과 경이
title: Machines built to imitate the living
content: Before the age of factories, craftsmen built figures that wrote, drew, played music, and seemed to breathe. These machines were shown to paying crowds across Europe, and although their makers were praised for skill, the praise carried something closer to unease. Their mechanisms were real feats. A figure that writes a line must lift the pen, place it, and press with changing force, and because the orders must be held somewhere, the best examples used stacks of shaped discs read by followers. The same principle appears later in programmable machinery, and historians of computing cite these figures as ancestors. Musical ones went further still. A figure playing a flute must rule the breath, the lips, and the fingers, and one famous example did all three with bellows and cams, making a sound that watchers called no different from a player. Its maker printed an account of the trouble, and that is among the earliest close descriptions of a machine copying what a body does. Fraud existed alongside the genuine work. A famous chess playing figure toured for decades and was at last shown to hide a person inside, and that exposure coloured how later crowds took everything of the kind. The public appetite for both the real and the fake was considerable. What the tradition finally produced was an argument rather than an entertainment. Because a machine could write, play, and seem to breathe, the line between mechanism and life became a question rather than a given, and eighteenth century writers followed that thought into print. The discomfort audiences reported is the same discomfort that convincing imitation still produces.

subject: 낭독회의 전통
title: Hearing an author read their own work
content: Public readings by authors are now routine, although the practice has a history in which the reading was the main event rather than a promotional appearance. Understanding what it once was explains why the form persists despite books being available to anybody. Nineteenth century readings were therefore performances. Authors toured, charged admission, and prepared their material carefully, cutting and rearranging for delivery, and the most successful earned more from reading than from writing. Contemporary accounts describe audiences of thousands and effects on listeners that no private reading produces. Their material was adapted for the occasion. An author preparing a passage for delivery shortens description, sharpens dialogue, and marks a script for emphasis and pause, so what the audience heard was a version made for the voice. Surviving marked copies show these decisions, and because they were made by the author, they are a source for how the writer understood their own work. Yet something is carried across that print cannot hold. Rhythm, emphasis, and which words the author regards as important all become audible, and listeners frequently report that a passage they had read many times sounded different, which is evidence that a text underdetermines its delivery. Recordings of authors reading are prized for exactly this reason. The modern form is smaller, and although the scale has changed, it keeps the essential feature. An audience gathers to hear a text in the presence of whoever made it, which is closer to the oral traditions that preceded printing than to private reading, and the persistence of the practice suggests it supplies something that the availability of the book does not.

subject: 웃음을 만드는 형식
title: The structures that produce laughter
content: Comic writing depends on structures that can be described and taught, which surprises people who assume that humour is a matter of temperament. Performers and writers work with a vocabulary of forms, and the forms recur across cultures and centuries with remarkable stability. Timing is structural rather than instinctive. A joke arrives at a moment when the audience has formed an expectation, and the interval before the reversal must be long enough for the expectation to settle and short enough that attention has not moved. Performers describe adjusting this by fractions of a second, and the same words delivered a beat early or late fail. The rule of three appears everywhere. Two instances establish a pattern and the third breaks it, which is the minimum required to set up an expectation and defeat it, and lists in comic writing are almost invariably three items long. Four is available and it dilutes; two does not establish enough. Reversal of status underlies a great deal. A figure of authority reduced, or somebody insignificant elevated, produces the incongruity that many theories of humour identify as the source, and the oldest surviving comic material uses exactly these arrangements. Callback rewards attention. Returning to an earlier element in a changed context produces a response larger than the element earned the first time, since the audience is pleased with itself for recognising it. Performers construct whole routines around this. What none of the structures supply is the material. Knowing the forms lets somebody build a joke that will work if the observation underneath it is good, and no structure rescues an observation that is not.

subject: 색채 영화의 도입
title: When films stopped being grey
content: Colour arrived in cinema slowly and was resisted for reasons that had nothing to do with technology. The processes existed decades before they became standard, and the delay was a matter of cost, aesthetics, and an argument about what film was for. Early methods were laborious. Frames were tinted, hand painted, or produced by processes requiring several strips of film exposed and combined, and each added expense and technical risk. The process that eventually dominated used a camera splitting light onto three negatives, which required special equipment, more light on set, and technicians supplied by the company that owned it. Studios rented rather than bought. Aesthetic resistance was substantial. Directors and cinematographers had spent decades developing an art of light and shadow in monochrome, and colour flattened those effects while drawing attention to itself. Early colour films were mostly musicals, fantasies, and spectacles, since colour was regarded as unsuitable for serious drama — a judgment that reversed within twenty years. Control was the practical difficulty. Colour records what is actually there, so sets, costumes, and makeup all had to be designed for it, and the company supplying the process employed consultants who advised on palettes and effectively influenced how films looked. Directors resented this. The transition completed for commercial reasons. Television broadcast in monochrome, so colour became the thing cinema could offer that home viewing could not, and within a decade black and white had become a deliberate choice rather than a default. It has remained available as exactly that, which is why a monochrome film made now reads as a statement in a way it could not have before.

subject: 스타 체계의 형성
title: How performers became the product
content: Early film companies did not name their actors. Performers were employees, credits were withheld deliberately, and audiences who wanted to identify a favourite had to invent names for them. The system that replaced this arrangement was built quickly once its commercial value became apparent. Audiences forced the change. Letters arrived asking about particular performers, and exhibitors reported that certain faces sold tickets regardless of the picture, so the information the studios had withheld turned out to be an asset. Once one company began promoting a named performer, the others followed within a year. Salaries rose accordingly. A performer whose name drew audiences could demand a share of what they generated, and the sums involved within a decade were extraordinary by any earlier standard for an entertainer. Studios responded by binding performers to long contracts that controlled what they appeared in and, in several documented cases, how they lived. The image was manufactured. Studios assigned names, invented biographies, arranged public appearances, and placed stories in a press that depended on access, so what audiences knew about a performer was produced by the same organisation that produced the films. Several performers described the arrangement as a second full time job. The system broke when the contracts did. Legal challenges and changes in how films were financed left performers free to work picture by picture, which increased their power and removed the machinery that had built the images. What replaced it is a looser arrangement in which performers manage their own visibility, and the underlying commercial fact — that a recognised face reduces the risk of an expensive production — has not changed at all.

subject: 의복의 사회사
title: What people were allowed to wear
content: Clothing has been regulated by law far more often than modern readers expect. Rules specifying what fabrics, colours, and ornaments each rank might wear were enacted repeatedly across Europe and Asia, and the frequency of their re-enactment shows that they were constantly broken. The purpose was legibility. Where rank determined obligations and privileges, being able to identify somebody's standing at a glance mattered, and a merchant dressing like a noble disrupted an order that everybody was supposed to be able to read. The laws targeted exactly the materials that new wealth could buy. Enforcement was uneven and largely symbolic. Penalties were fines, which the wealthy could pay, so the rules functioned as a tax on display rather than a prohibition, and several jurisdictions collected substantial revenue this way. Records of prosecutions are a useful source for what people were actually wearing. Trade complicated everything. Imported textiles arrived faster than laws could name them, and prohibitions on foreign cloth were also protectionist measures for domestic weavers, so a single statute frequently served status, morality, and trade policy at once. Untangling the motives requires reading the debates rather than the text. The laws faded as the orders they marked did. Where wealth rather than birth determined standing, and where anybody could buy what they could afford, the rules became unenforceable and were repealed or ignored. What replaced them is informal and no less effective, since dress still signals position reliably, and the signals are now enforced by recognition rather than by statute.

subject: 술을 나누는 의례
title: The rules that govern a shared drink
content: Almost every culture that produced alcohol also produced rules about how it is served and consumed, and the rules are remarkably elaborate given the simplicity of the act. They govern who pours, who drinks first, how a vessel is held, and what is said, and members follow them without instruction. Pouring for oneself is discouraged in many traditions. Where somebody else fills your cup and you fill theirs, the drinking becomes an exchange rather than a consumption, and attention is required throughout, since noticing an empty cup is part of the obligation. Traditions with this rule report that it slows the pace and keeps the group together. Order encodes standing. Who is served first, who initiates, and who may decline all follow rank, age, or relationship, and the sequence is a public statement about the group that everybody present can read. Getting it wrong is noticed immediately, which is why visitors find these occasions stressful. The toast is nearly universal. Raising vessels together marks a beginning, makes the group a unit, and frequently carries a statement of what the occasion is for, and the practice appears independently in traditions with no contact. Several explanations have been offered, including the practical one that a shared moment establishes that nobody has poisoned anything. Refusal is where the rules become visible. Somebody declining is declining more than a drink, since the offer was an inclusion, and traditions accordingly develop conventions for refusing without insult — accepting and not drinking, or naming a reason that everybody accepts. The elaboration of those conventions is a reliable indicator of how strong the underlying obligation is.

subject: 장난감이 담은 시대
title: What children's playthings record
content: Toys survive in quantity from the past two centuries and in fragments from much earlier, and they are unusually informative as historical evidence because they were made to be handled by people nobody was trying to impress. Miniatures record the adult world. Dolls' houses reproduce room arrangements, furniture, and utensils in detail, and several surviving examples are the best available evidence for how households of their period were actually furnished, since real interiors were rebuilt while the models were kept. Toy vehicles, tools, and shops do the same for work. Expectations are visible in what was made for whom. Toys directed at girls and boys diverged sharply during the nineteenth century and the division has been mapped through catalogues, which show a period of considerable separation, a partial convergence, and a re-separation in recent decades that surprised researchers who expected a trend. Materials date the object and shape the play. Wood, tin, celluloid, and injection moulded plastic each permitted different forms, and the shift to plastic in the mid twentieth century made complex shapes cheap, which changed what a toy could be and made them disposable for the first time. Survival is therefore biased toward the earlier materials. Wear is evidence too. A toy played with heavily and repaired repeatedly tells a different story from one kept in a box, and museums increasingly display the worn examples for exactly this reason. What such objects finally record is a version of childhood that adults constructed. The toys tell us what children were given rather than what they wanted, and the difference between the two is visible in the ones that were used until they broke.

subject: 목욕 문화의 건축
title: Buildings made for washing together
content: Public bathing produced some of the most elaborate architecture in several civilizations, and the buildings tell us that washing was rarely only washing. The scale of the structures, and what else they contained, indicate an institution closer to a civic centre than to a facility. Roman examples included exercise grounds, libraries, gardens, and halls for conversation alongside a graded sequence of rooms at different temperatures. The engineering was substantial: furnaces heated air circulated beneath floors and inside walls, aqueducts supplied the water, and drains removed it, so a bath complex required an infrastructure that only a wealthy city could sustain. Their ruins are among the largest surviving Roman structures. The sequence of rooms was itself designed. Moving from warm to hot to cold produced a physiological effect that the culture regarded as healthful, and the architecture enforced the order, so bathers followed a route rather than choosing. Traditions elsewhere organised the sequence differently and were equally specific about it. Social function shaped the plan. Where bathing was mixed, the arrangement differed from where it was separated by hour or by building, and changes in practice are visible in remodelling. Several complexes were divided or rebuilt as attitudes changed, which is legible in the masonry. The tradition persisted where the water was. Regions with hot springs developed bathing cultures independently, with their own architecture and their own conventions about silence, order, and what may be discussed, and several of those traditions are continuous into the present. Where the water had to be heated, the practice depended on fuel and on public investment, and it ended when either failed.

subject: 순례와 여행의 차이
title: Travelling toward something rather than away
content: A pilgrimage and a journey may cover the same ground and differ entirely in what they are. The distinction lies in the destination having a meaning that the traveller accepts before setting out, which reorganises every part of the trip around arrival. Difficulty is a feature rather than a cost. Many traditions specify that at least part of the route be walked, that comfort be limited, or that particular hardships be accepted, and pilgrims who arrive by convenient transport report feeling that something was missing. The effort is understood to be part of what is offered, which no ordinary journey requires. The route is prescribed and shared. Pilgrims follow paths that others have followed for centuries, stop where others stopped, and encounter the same landmarks, so the journey connects them to everybody who made it before. Infrastructure grew along these routes — hostels, chapels, markets — and several major roads across Europe and Asia exist because of them. Companionship is structural. Pilgrims travel among strangers with a shared purpose, ordinary distinctions of standing are suspended for the duration, and the resulting temporary community has been studied as a social form in its own right. Accounts from many traditions describe the same phenomenon in similar terms. Tourism has grown around the same sites, and the two activities now share the routes. Pilgrims frequently object, and their objection is not to the presence of others but to a different relation to the destination: somebody who arrives to look at a place has not made the journey the place was built to receive. Several traditions have responded by marking a final portion that must be walked, which restores the distinction without excluding anybody.

subject: 사진관과 초상의 대중화
title: When ordinary people could own their own image
content: Before photography, having one's likeness made required a painter and money, so most people lived and died with no image of themselves. Within about thirty years of the first practical process, portraits had become affordable to a large part of the population, and the consequences reached well beyond the pictures. The studio was a specific kind of place. Long exposures required strong light and a stillness that people could not maintain unaided, so studios were built with glass roofs and equipped with stands that held the sitter's head, and the resulting stiffness of early portraits is a technical artefact rather than a period manner. As exposures shortened, poses relaxed visibly. Conventions were borrowed from painting. Backdrops, columns, drapery, and props signalled standing exactly as they had in painted portraits, so a working family could be photographed against a painted library. Critics of the period mocked this and it was doing something real, since the sitters were claiming a form of representation that had belonged to their social superiors. Small formats made the images circulate. Cards the size of a visiting card were produced in quantity, exchanged among families, and collected in albums, and the same format carried images of public figures, so a household album might hold relatives beside a monarch. This mixture of the private and the public was new. The lasting change was in memory. Families acquired a visual record across generations, faces of the dead remained available, and the resulting relationship to one's own past has no earlier equivalent. What the studios sold was inexpensive and its effect on how people understood their own lives was considerable.

subject: 우표와 수집의 심리
title: Why people complete sets
content: Collecting is close to universal and its objects are frequently worthless outside the practice. Postage stamps supply the clearest case: mass produced, printed by the million, and valued according to rules that only collectors recognise. Understanding what drives the activity illuminates a great deal about how people relate to objects. Completeness organises everything. A set defined by a catalogue creates a gap that can be filled, and the pleasure reported is not in owning any single item but in the set approaching wholeness. Publishers of catalogues therefore define what a collection is, and their decisions about what counts as a distinct item have created and destroyed markets. Scarcity is constructed rather than found. A stamp is valuable because few survive in good condition, and condition is judged by criteria the community established, so two objects identical in origin may differ enormously in value according to a grading scale that exists only by agreement. Newcomers find this arbitrary and it is entirely consistent. Knowledge is the real currency. Serious collectors accumulate expertise about printings, papers, watermarks, and errors, and the ability to identify what others miss is where the satisfaction lies. Several collectors have described the objects as an occasion for the study rather than its point. Errors are prized above correct examples, which is revealing. A stamp printed upside down is worth far more than the millions printed properly, because scarcity has become the whole of the value, and the aesthetic and functional qualities of the object contribute nothing. Any theory of collecting must account for this, and the accounts that succeed treat the practice as a system of meaning that participants build rather than as an appreciation of things.

subject: 달력 그림의 유통
title: Pictures that hung in every house
content: For much of the twentieth century the most widely spread pictures in many countries were printed on calendars. Firms gave them away, homes hung them in kitchens and sheds, and they were swapped each year, which means a vast body of popular imagery went round and almost none of it lasts. The trade explains the form. A calendar was an advertisement, so the picture had to be pleasing enough that somebody would hang it and mild enough not to offend, and the firm that paid wanted its name seen without taking over. This made a look one can recognise: pleasing subjects, sound handling, bright colour, and nothing that would start an argument. Certain subjects recurred across countries. Landscapes, children, animals, and tidy scenes of home life turned up everywhere, and that sameness suggests the constraint rather than any local taste was doing the choosing. Traditions with their own strong picture rules took them into the format, which made mixtures that art historians now study. The artists were mostly anonymous and some were not. Several painters lived on this work while pursuing other things, and a few became well known for the calendars, though the kind has never carried standing. Original paintings made for reproduction were frequently discarded once photographed. Survival is accidental and biased. What is left is what somebody kept for a reason — a striking picture, a local scene, a firm that mattered to the house — so what survives gives a false picture of what actually hung on walls. Collections assembled recently have begun to correct this, and researchers using them report a considerably wider range of imagery than the familiar examples suggest.

subject: 초상 사진의 자세
title: How a photographer arranges a person
content: A photographic portrait looks like a record of somebody and is a construction. The position of the body, the angle of the head, where the eyes look, and what the hands do are all decided, usually by the photographer, and the resulting image says as much about the conventions applied as about the sitter. The angle of the face is the most consequential choice. A head turned slightly produces a shape that most traditions consider more agreeable than a full frontal view, and photographers learn which side of a given face is more symmetrical. A full frontal portrait reads as confrontational or official, which is why identification photographs use it and why portraits intending warmth do not. The eyes determine the relation. Looking at the lens creates an address to the viewer; looking away creates an observed subject who is unaware, and the two produce entirely different pictures of the same person. Portraits of powerful figures overwhelmingly use the first; portraits intended as studies frequently use the second. Hands are the standing difficulty. Photographers describe them as the hardest element, since hands that are doing nothing look awkward and hands that are posed look posed, and the usual solutions — holding something, resting somewhere, partly out of frame — are visible across the whole history of the form. Height of the camera carries meaning that viewers read without noticing. A lens below eye level enlarges and elevates the subject, and one above diminishes them, and the effect operates whether or not anybody intended it. Photographers of public figures are frequently instructed about this, and the instruction is a request about how the person will be perceived rather than about how they will look.

subject: 조명 색이 만드는 감정
title: How coloured light changes a scene
content: Stage and screen lighting uses colour on purpose, and its effects are reliable enough to be taught. What makes this practice interesting is that audiences respond without noticing its cause, crediting the scene with what the light supplied. Colour temperature does most of this work. Light shifted toward blue reads as cold, distant, and frequently nocturnal, while light shifted toward amber reads as warm, close, and domestic, and the associations are strong enough that a single scene lit both ways will be described in different emotional terms by viewers who could not say why. Their origin is probably in daylight and firelight. Saturation carries a second meaning of its own. Strongly coloured light reads as unreal, so heightened or dreamlike sequences use it while ordinary ones do not, and the threshold at which an audience begins to register the colour as a device rather than as a condition is something designers learn by experience. Contrast between two such sources creates space. Lighting a figure with one colour from the front and another from behind separates them from the background and suggests two sources, which the eye reads as depth even on a flat screen. Most ordinary lighting setups are built from exactly this principle. Skin sets the limit on all of it. Faces tolerate a narrow range before they look unwell, and the range differs by complexion, which has produced a documented history of film stock and lighting practice calibrated for lighter skin and failing on darker. Practitioners raised this for decades before the industry responded, and the correction involved both technology and training. What the whole practice demonstrates is that a viewer's emotional reading of a scene is partly manufactured by a technician nobody credits.

subject: 합창 지휘와 호흡
title: Making many people breathe as one
content: Conducting a choir differs from conducting instruments in one decisive respect: the instrument is the body, and its limits are the singer's limits. A conductor who ignores breath is asking for something that cannot be delivered, and most of the craft follows from that constraint. Breathing must be planned. A long phrase exceeds what any singer can sustain, so the conductor decides where breaths fall, and in a large group the decision can be staggered so that individuals breathe at different moments while the sound continues unbroken. This technique makes possible phrases of any length, and it must be rehearsed, since singers left to their own judgment will breathe together and the line will break. The conductor's own breath leads. A preparatory gesture that includes an intake tells the choir when and how much to take, and the character of that breath — quick and shallow, slow and deep — determines the attack that follows. Choral conductors describe this as the single most important gesture they make. Vowels determine blend. A chord in which singers form vowels differently will not blend regardless of tuning, so a great deal of rehearsal concerns the shape of the mouth rather than pitch, and choirs from different traditions are recognisable by their vowel colour before anything else. Tuning follows the ear rather than an instrument. Unaccompanied singers adjust to each other continuously, and a good choir will drift from any fixed reference toward intervals that sound purer, which is a technical virtue and a practical problem when an instrument enters. Conductors manage this by choosing when to give a reference and when to let the ensemble find its own.

subject: 전시 도록의 편집
title: The book that outlives the exhibition
content: An exhibition lasts a few months while its catalogue lasts indefinitely. For most people that book is the exhibition, since far more will read it than will visit, and this imbalance shapes how such volumes are put together. Such a catalogue does several jobs at once. It records what was shown, supplies scholarship that the wall labels could not carry, reproduces the works, and argues the case that the exhibition was making. These purposes conflict, because a record wants completeness while an argument wants selection, and editors weigh them constantly. Their scholarship is frequently substantial. Assembling works that are normally scattered permits comparisons nobody could make otherwise, and the resulting essays sometimes settle questions that had been open for decades. Several catalogues are cited as primary references in their fields long after the exhibition closed. Reproduction is their persistent problem. A photograph of a painting differs from the painting in scale, surface, and colour, and the printing process introduces further shifts, so a reader forms an impression of a work they have not seen. Publishers invest heavily in colour accuracy for exactly this reason, and specialists still describe the results as approximations. Their sequence carries the argument. The order in which works are reproduced makes a case, and it usually follows the hang, so a reader walks the exhibition on paper. Where the two diverge, the editor has decided that the book should argue differently from the rooms, which is a decision worth noticing. What the form finally produces is a curious object: a permanent record of something temporary, made by people who know that their book will be consulted long after nobody remembers the walls.

subject: 사진의 프레임이 배제하는 것
title: Everything the photograph left out
content: A photograph shows what was in front of the lens within a rectangle. Everything outside that rectangle existed and is absent, and the viewer has no way to know what it was, which makes the frame the most consequential decision a photographer makes and the least visible one. Cropping is an argument. A demonstration photographed tightly appears crowded and photographed widely appears sparse, and both images are accurate records of the same event. Newspapers have been criticised for exactly this, and the criticism is difficult to answer, since no framing is neutral and the photographer must choose one. What is just outside frequently matters most. A portrait of somebody working may exclude the conditions they work in; a landscape may exclude the road behind the photographer. Several documentary photographers have deliberately included such elements to resist the convention, producing images that look careless and are making a point about what the tradition usually removes. The frame also creates relations that did not exist. Two things placed within one rectangle read as connected, and a photographer can suggest a relationship by position alone without any claim being made, which is a technique used in advertising continuously and in journalism more than is acknowledged. Time is framed as well. A photograph selects an instant from a continuous event, and an expression held for a fraction of a second can be presented as a person's attitude. Public figures are photographed constantly for exactly this reason, and the resulting images are chosen by editors from thousands. What a viewer receives is therefore doubly selected, and neither selection announces itself.

subject: 연대기 삽화의 시각 관습
title: How illustrated chronicles show time passing
content: Medieval and early modern chronicles were frequently illustrated, and their pictures follow conventions that a modern reader misreads without knowing them. The images are not attempts at accurate depiction, and treating them as such produces confident errors about how people looked and lived. Several moments appear in one picture. A figure may be shown arriving, acting, and departing within a single frame, so the image represents a sequence rather than an instant, and a reader who assumes a single moment sees a crowd where there was one person. This convention is universal enough that its abandonment in favour of a single instant is itself a datable change. Scale indicates importance. Rulers are larger than attendants, and the size difference encodes standing rather than distance, so a picture in which a king towers over a city is not making a claim about his height. The same convention appears in many unrelated traditions, which suggests it is a natural solution rather than a borrowed one. Dress and setting are contemporary. Illustrators showed ancient events with figures in the clothing of their own day, in buildings of their own period, using weapons they had seen, and this was not ignorance but a convention treating the past as continuous with the present. It makes such images excellent evidence for the illustrator's time and worthless for the events depicted. Symbols carry identity. Individuals are recognised by attributes rather than by features — a crown, an instrument, an animal — so faces are generic and the identifying information sits elsewhere. Reading these pictures therefore requires knowing the attribute system, which was common knowledge when they were made and must now be reconstructed.

subject: 목공 접합의 원리
title: Joining wood so that it can move
content: Wood expands and contracts across the grain as humidity changes, and it does so with enough force to split anything that restrains it. Every traditional joint is a response to this fact, and the sophistication of the traditions comes from managing movement rather than preventing it. The direction of movement is predictable. A board changes width considerably and length almost not at all, so a joint connecting two pieces whose grain runs in different directions must allow one to move while the other does not. Fixing such a joint rigidly guarantees a split, and furniture made without this understanding fails within a few seasons. Frame and panel construction solves it elegantly. A thin panel sits in a groove within a frame without being fastened, so it expands and contracts freely while the frame holds the shape, and the arrangement appears in door and chest construction across many unconnected traditions. Its invention was a genuine advance. Interlocking joints supply strength without glue. Dovetails resist being pulled apart in one direction by their geometry alone, and traditions working before reliable adhesives depended entirely on such shapes, cutting them by hand to fits measured in fractions of a millimetre. Several East Asian traditions developed joints of extraordinary complexity that permit disassembly, which suits buildings expected to be repaired. Fasteners changed the calculation and not the physics. Screws and modern adhesives allow rigid connections that older joinery avoided, and furniture assembled this way still splits when the wood moves, which is why manufacturers use materials that do not move at all. The traditional joints survive where solid wood is used, because the problem they solve has not gone anywhere.

subject: 번안과 개작의 경계
title: When a translation becomes a new work
content: A text moved into another language can be rendered closely, adapted freely, or reset entirely in a new place with new names. These are different activities, and traditions have drawn the lines between them differently, which produces genuine confusion about what a reader is holding. Close translation aims to carry the original across. Its practitioners accept awkwardness where the languages resist each other, on the ground that smoothing it away conceals the difference between the cultures, and readers of such versions encounter something that reads as foreign. This is a deliberate effect with a long history of defence. Free adaptation aims at the effect rather than the words. A joke that depends on a pun becomes a different joke, a reference nobody will recognise becomes one they will, and the resulting text produces in its readers something like what the original produced in its own. Defenders argue that fidelity to effect is the truer fidelity, and the argument is old and unresolved. Relocation goes further. Nineteenth century adaptations frequently moved a novel to the translating country entirely, changing names, settings, and customs, and readers encountered a domestic story that happened to have a foreign origin. Whole literatures entered new languages this way before close translation became the norm. The practice has not disappeared. Film and theatre relocate constantly, children's literature is adapted heavily, and the version most readers of a foreign classic encounter is frequently an abridgement made for a purpose nobody stated. What the categories finally require is disclosure, since a reader who believes they are reading one thing while holding another has been misled about something they would have wanted to know.

subject: 라디오 드라마의 소리
title: Building a scene from sound alone
content: Drama made for listening supplies no image, and traditions that developed it worked out how to place a listener in a space using nothing but what can be heard. The techniques are precise and largely unnoticed by audiences, which is the mark of their success. Distance is created by level and by reverberation. A voice recorded close and dry is beside the listener; the same voice further from the microphone in a live room is across a hall, and moving between the two within a scene tells the audience that somebody walked away. Listeners construct the room without being told anything about it. Effects establish place economically. A few seconds of the right ambience — a street, a kitchen, weather — locates a scene faster than any description, and the tradition learned to place these under the first line rather than before it, since a listener who has heard nothing yet has nothing to attach the sound to. Silence is the strongest resource and the riskiest, because a listener cannot tell it from a fault. Writers therefore surround it with something faint, so the absence of speech reads as a pause rather than as a failure of the broadcast, and this small technical necessity has shaped how such drama is written. Voices must be distinguishable. A cast whose voices resemble each other confuses a listener who has no faces to consult, so casting attends to contrast in a way that visual media need not, and scripts name characters more often than natural speech would. What the form finally exploits is that a listener builds the picture. Practitioners have long argued that this produces images no budget could match, and the claim is difficult to test and consistent with what audiences report.
